title: Frank Johnson, Leader of the Brass Band of the 128th Regiment in Saratoga, with his wife, Helen
observations: Two full-length figures in solid black cut paper stand in profile on a plain buff mount: a man at left playing a keyed bugle, a woman at right in a long full skirt.
Interior detail is almost absent; only a few fine white lines mark coat seams, hair and the folds of the skirt.
The outlines carry the information: the raised instrument, the man's coat tails, the woman's hair bun and the bell of her skirt.
Handwritten labels below each figure name Frank Johnson and Helen Johnson of Philadelphia, with Saratoga dates of 1842 and 1844.

techniques.effect: With interior detail removed, each person is identified by contour alone, the bugle, coat tails and skirt shape, so the pair reads at once against the pale ground.

summary: A pair of nineteenth-century cut-paper portraits shows how a profile outline alone can identify a person and what they do.
teaching_value: The classic cut-paper silhouette: full-length, profile, no interior modelling. A direct model for icon and pictogram design where a figure must read by outline.
ambiguity: The two figures were cut two years apart and mounted together, so their spacing reflects the mount, not one composed scene.

title: South Sea Islanders
observations: Black cut-paper figures stand and move across a pale sepia wash landscape with palms, a mountain and a wide plain.
In the foreground one figure swings a club-like object overhead while holding the wrist of a seated figure; their limbs and the weapon read only as outline.
Smaller black figures with spears and feathered headdresses recede toward the horizon, the smallest in the far middle distance.
The landscape is painted in soft brown wash with visible brushwork, while the figures are flat and uniformly black.

techniques.effect: Flat black figures against a soft painted ground read as clear gestures and poses before any detail, so the action is legible at a glance.
Figures shrinking from foreground to horizon set up near, middle and far planes even though each figure is flat.

summary: A cut-paper scene set on a painted wash shows silhouettes carrying action and depth through outline and size alone.
teaching_value: Silhouettes used for a whole narrative scene rather than a portrait, with depth made by diminishing size.
ambiguity: The scene is a European artist's depiction of Pacific Islanders and of a violent encounter; it records the maker's view, not documented events. Cut figures combined with a painted background are a hybrid technique.

title: Cinderella, silhouette illustration
observations: A girl in a full skirt leaps with both arms raised, drawn as a solid black shape on white; ribbons on her arms and a bow in her hair are readable only by outline.
Two small black dogs jump toward her, one from the lower left and one from the right.
Black trees with lacy foliage stand at both sides, and a small black disc sits in the upper left sky.
The white ground is left open between the figures, so each shape stays mostly separate from the others.

techniques.effect: Pure black shapes on white make the pose and the dogs read instantly from contour, keeping the scene simple and graphic.
Raised arms, the lifted skirt and the dogs caught mid-jump freeze a leap, so the picture reads as movement.

summary: A 1919 book illustration tells a lively moment with black silhouette, outline and pose alone.
teaching_value: Illustration silhouette with motion: shows how separated, unoverlapped outlines keep a busy scene readable.
ambiguity: The black disc could be a sun or a moon; nothing in the image settles it.

title: Neujahrsglückwunsch (New Year's greeting), 1800
observations: An oval wreath of black cut-paper leaves encircles a black landscape scene on white paper, with an eagle with spread wings cut at the top.
Inside the oval a temple, trees, a castle on a crag, a carriage with horses and a sailing boat are all cut as flat black shapes, readable by their outlines.
Fine cuts inside the black areas open small white gaps for windows, waves, rocks and lettering.
Tools, weapons and emblems are scattered around the outside of the wreath.

techniques.effect: Every element is a flat black shape against white, so the scene is read from contour and cut openings, not from shading.
The oval wreath encloses the landscape like a window and separates the scene from the emblems around it.

summary: A cut-paper greeting from 1800 builds a whole landscape from black silhouettes inside an oval wreath.
teaching_value: Shows the range of silhouette: architecture, vehicles and plants all made legible by outline and small cut openings.
ambiguity: Parts are backed with colour and gold, so not every area is pure black and white; the emblems and small lettering are hard to read at this size and are not interpreted.

title: The Moon-Viewing Promontory, from One Hundred Views of Famous Places in Edo
observations: An open room with a green tatami floor, wooden posts and ceiling frames a view of the bay, with many boats on the horizon and a full moon at upper left.
On the translucent paper screen at the left edge a dark grey shadow of a figure with an elaborate hairstyle and hair ornaments is cast, with no interior detail.
At the right edge only part of a seated person's clothing is visible, cut by the doorframe.
A pine branch and a potted plant on the veranda sit in front of the room at lower right.

techniques.effect: Posts, ceiling and floor edges enclose the bay, so the moonlit water reads as a picture within the picture.
The figure on the screen is known only by its outline, suggesting a person present but unseen.

summary: A woodblock print frames a moonlit bay through a room, with a guest present only as a shadow on a paper screen.
teaching_value: A silhouette made by a cast shadow on a screen rather than a cut shape: presence without detail.
ambiguity: The shadow is softer and greyer than a cut or backlit silhouette; who the figure is cannot be told from the pixels.

title: Der Auserwählte (The Chosen One)
observations: Six standing winged figures in near-identical long pale blue robes and white cloaks are spaced evenly across the picture, each with long dark hair and a similar upright pose.
A small nude child kneels on the ground in the lower centre facing a sapling; it is the only figure that is low, unclothed and turned toward the others.
Hands and heads vary slightly: some figures hold small flowers, some fold their hands at the chest, and heads tilt different ways.
The figures float above a meadow with small white flowers, with a band of distant landscape and sky behind.

techniques.effect: The evenly repeated robed figures set up a strong expectation, and the single small kneeling child breaks it, so the eye goes to the child first.
Near-identical vertical figures at regular intervals make a steady beat across the canvas, with small variations in hands and heads.

summary: A symbolist painting repeats six almost identical robed figures and breaks the series with one small kneeling child.
teaching_value: A clean odd-one-out in painting: same colour, size and pose repeated six times, one figure different in size, pose and colour.
ambiguity: The meaning of the scene is not established from the pixels; this reading is about structure only. Colour may differ from the original painting in this photograph.

title: Stephoidea, plate from Kunstformen der Natur
observations: Twelve white skeletal radiolarian forms are arranged in rows on a black ground, most built from open rings with spiky branches.
At the centre one form is a closed, round latticed sphere with a pink interior, unlike the open rings around it.
Two forms, top centre and bottom centre, are surrounded by many small yellow dots and have pink and orange cores.

techniques.effect: Among many open, spiky ring shapes the single closed sphere breaks the series and pulls the eye to the centre of the plate.
Bright white forms on a black ground make every outline stand out sharply.

summary: A 1904 scientific plate repeats related forms on black, with one closed sphere at the centre breaking the series.
teaching_value: Repetition with variation in a specimen plate: shows how one change of shape inside a family of forms becomes the focal point.
ambiguity: The forms vary throughout (repetition with variation), so the central sphere is the clearest break rather than the only one; the two dotted forms also stand apart.

title: Procession of a Daimyo
observations: About a dozen men stride toward the left in one dense group, all in the same pose with the left leg forward, black socks, sandals and swords at the waist.
Most wear black outer jackets over patterned robes; one man near the front wears a pale green robe and carries a tall feathered spear, and the leader carries a tall black cased object.
Shaved crowns with topknots repeat at two heights across the sheet.
The paper ground is left plain, with no setting.

techniques.effect: The repeated stride and black jackets set a marching rhythm; the pale green robe and tall spear break it and mark one man out at the front.
Repeated legs, swords and heads at regular intervals make the group read as one marching column.

summary: A seventeenth-century woodblock print repeats striding figures in black jackets and breaks the pattern with one pale robe near the front.
teaching_value: Odd one out inside a crowd: colour change in one repeated figure among many identical poses.
ambiguity: Two leading figures differ (the pale green robe and the pale-robed leader), so the break is shared rather than single; the men's ranks are not established from the image.

title: Ballet at the Paris Opéra
observations: A tight line of dancers in white tutus stands overlapping right of centre on the stage, their dark hair and skirts merging into one mass.
One dancer poses at left with an arm raised, separated from the line by open stage floor, with two fainter dancers just behind her.
Heads of spectators fill the bottom edge, cut off by the frame, and the scroll of a double bass rises at the right edge.
The stage scenery behind is loosely handled in green and blue.

techniques.effect: Packing the corps into one overlapping line and setting the soloist apart across empty floor makes the line read as one unit and the soloist as separate.
Audience heads and an instrument cut by the frame put the viewer in the seats, glimpsing the stage between them.

summary: A pastel of a ballet groups the corps into one overlapping line apart from a soloist, seen past cropped heads in the audience.
teaching_value: Grouping by spacing alone: same costumes, but the gap decides who belongs together.
ambiguity: Two faint dancers stand behind the soloist, so she is not entirely alone; the cropped heads also form a foreground layer, which is not counted here.

title: Yellow Dancers (In the Wings)
observations: Three dancers in yellow tutus fill the right two-thirds of the canvas, pressed together shoulder to shoulder.
The right-hand dancer is cut by the right edge, and the skirts run off the bottom edge.
At left a painted stage flat hides most of the stage; only several pairs of bare legs and feet show beneath it.
The tutus are brushed loosely in yellow-green, while faces and arms are more defined.

techniques.effect: Cutting the dancers at the edges and showing others only as feet under a flat gives a glimpsed, offstage view rather than a posed portrait.
The three dancers huddled into one mass read as a single group, separate from the anonymous feet beyond the flat.

summary: A backstage painting crops dancers at the edges and shows others only as feet below a stage flat.
teaching_value: Cropping as viewpoint: the frame cuts figures the way a casual glance would.
ambiguity: The loose skirts against more defined faces could also be read as selective focus; it is not counted here.

title: Kinryūsan Temple at Asakusa, from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo"
observations: A huge red and black paper lantern hangs from the top edge, cut off by the frame so only its lower half shows.
A red and green gate post runs the full height of the left edge, also cut by the frame.
Through this opening a snowy temple precinct with a red gate, a five-storey pagoda and small figures with umbrellas recedes into falling snow.

techniques.effect: Cutting the lantern and post at the edges puts the viewer right under the gate, so the near objects feel immediate and the precinct far away.
The post and lantern form an inner frame around the snowy view of the temple.

summary: A woodblock print crops a giant lantern and gate post at the edges to frame a snowy temple view.
teaching_value: Foreground cropped by the frame: a fragment of a large object implies scale and places the viewer.
ambiguity: The large lantern also creates scale contrast with the small figures; only cropping and framing are counted.

title: Fukagawa Susaki and Jumantsubo (Fukagawa Susaki Jumantsubo), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)"
observations: A large eagle dives from the top of the sheet, seen from above and behind, its wings cut by the top and right edges.
Far below, a snowy flat plain with small trees, water and a tiny floating tub spreads to a horizon with a distant white mountain.
Sky fills the space between the eagle and the land, flecked with falling snow.

techniques.effect: Looking down on the land from beside the eagle gives a bird's-eye view: the plain becomes a small pattern and the viewer shares the bird's height.
Cutting the wings at the frame edges makes the eagle too big to fit, increasing its closeness and force.
The huge near eagle against the tiny landscape below makes the distance dramatic.

summary: A woodblock print views a snowy plain from the height of a diving eagle whose wings are cut by the frame.
teaching_value: High vantage made with a single near element: the eagle places the viewer in the air.
ambiguity: The vantage is implied by the eagle over the land rather than strict perspective; the plain is drawn fairly flat.

title: Sir John Herschel (1792-1871)
observations: The face is the sharpest area: wrinkles, eyes and fine strands of white hair are clearly resolved.
The white hair at the edges and the dark cloak below are softer and lose detail, merging into the background.
The background is a nearly uniform dark brown with no visible setting.

techniques.effect: Only the face is crisp; the softer hair and cloak dissolve into darkness, so attention settles on the eyes and lined skin.
The lit face and white hair against near-black surroundings make the head the brightest area.

summary: A Victorian portrait photograph keeps the face sharp while hair and cloak soften into a dark ground.
teaching_value: Selective focus before modern lenses: sharpness concentrated on the face of a sitter.
ambiguity: The softness may come from lens, focus and exposure in a wet collodion print rather than a chosen shallow depth of field; the reading is about the visible result.

title: Julia Jackson
observations: The head fills most of the frame, cropped at the top of the hair and just below the neck.
The eyes, nose and mouth are fairly sharp, while the long hair at the sides is soft and blurred.
The background is dark and mottled; only the face and neck catch light.

techniques.effect: Filling the frame with the face removes setting and body, making the portrait direct and close.
With the features sharper than the soft hair, the eye settles on the face and gaze.

summary: A close Victorian portrait photograph fills the frame with a face, softening the hair around it.
teaching_value: A frame-filling head: cropping and soft surroundings direct attention to the gaze.
ambiguity: The face is not fully sharp either, so the focus difference is moderate; the second Cameron portrait in the pack differs in crop and lighting.
